A linear map $T:V\to W$ ([[def-linear-map]]) between inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) is a **linear isometry** if

$$\lVert Tv\rVert=\lVert v\rVert$$

for every $v\in V$, where the norm is the induced norm [[def-inner-product-norm]]. An invertible linear isometry from a real finite-dimensional inner product space to itself is an **orthogonal operator**; over $\mathbb C$ it is a **unitary operator**.

Equivalently, once the finite-dimensional characterisation is proved, orthogonal and unitary operators are the endomorphisms satisfying $T^*T=TT^*=I$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided monoidal category with braiding $c$ and let
$X\in\mathcal C$. For every $n\ge2$ there is a canonical group homomorphism

$$\rho_n\colon B_n\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}_{\mathcal C}(X^{\otimes n})$$

characterized by the property that $\rho_n(\sigma_i)$ is the local braiding of
the $i$-th and $(i+1)$-st tensor factors: in a strict model
$\rho_n(\sigma_i)=1_X^{\otimes(i-1)}\otimes c_{X,X}\otimes1_X^{\otimes(n-i-1)}$,
while in general $c_{X,X}$ is transported by the associativity isomorphisms and
the result is independent of those choices by braided coherence
([[thm-braided-coherence-via-underlying-braids]]). The actions are compatible
with the standard inclusions $\iota_n\colon B_n\to B_{n+1}$ for $n\ge1$:

$$\rho_{n+1}(\iota_n(\beta))=\rho_n(\beta)\otimes1_X .$$

For $n=0,1$, define $\rho_n$ to be the unique homomorphism from the
trivial group $B_n$ to $\operatorname{Aut}(X^{\otimes n})$, with
$X^{\otimes0}=\mathbf 1$. There are no local generators in these cases.
At $n=0$, let $\lambda_X:\mathbf 1\otimes X\to X$ be the left unitor. Compatibility means

$$\rho_1(\iota_0(e))=\lambda_X(\rho_0(e)\otimes1_X)\lambda_X^{-1}=1_X .$$

For $n=1$ the preceding compatibility formula is literal because both sides
are the identity of $X\otimes X$.

The statement holds for the braiding of [[def-braided-monoidal-category]] with
no choice principle.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-fusion-and-multifusion-category]]. A **dagger structure** assigns to every
morphism $f:X\to Y$ a morphism $f^\dagger:Y\to X$, conjugate-linearly, with
$(g\circ f)^\dagger=f^\dagger\circ g^\dagger$ and
$(f^\dagger)^\dagger=f$. A **unitary fusion category** is such a fusion
category equipped with this dagger so that every morphism space is a
finite-dimensional normed space, composition is submultiplicative,
$\|f^\dagger\|=\|f\|$, and $\|f^\dagger f\|=\|f\|^2$. Thus each
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra.
Positive endomorphisms are the elements of its usual $C^*$-positive cone
(equivalently $u^\dagger u$ for an endomorphism $u$); in particular, if $c$ is
simple and $\operatorname{End}(c)=\mathbb C\operatorname{id}_c$, then
$\lambda\operatorname{id}_c$ is positive exactly when $\lambda\ge0$. For any
morphism $f:X\to Y$, $f^\dagger f$ is positive in $\operatorname{End}(X)$;
also require $f^\dagger f=0$ to imply $f=0$. Semisimple direct-sum
decompositions can be chosen orthogonally:
their inclusions $i_j$ satisfy $i_j^\dagger i_k=0$ for $j\ne k$,
$i_j^\dagger i_j=\operatorname{id}$, and $\sum_j i_j i_j^\dagger=\operatorname{id}$.
Tensor product preserves daggers:
$(f\otimes g)^\dagger=f^\dagger\otimes g^\dagger$. Its associator and unit
constraints are **unitary**, meaning $\alpha^\dagger=\alpha^{-1}$,
$\lambda^\dagger=\lambda^{-1}$, and $\rho^\dagger=\rho^{-1}$.

The underlying fusion category is rigid, so its evaluation and coevaluation
morphisms satisfy the duality zig-zag identities. Those morphisms are not
required to be unitary isomorphisms. A braiding is additional structure; when
it is specified as a **unitary braiding**, each component satisfies
$c_{X,Y}^\dagger=c_{X,Y}^{-1}$. Positivity and unitarity are extra structure,
not consequences of the fusion rules or of the braid relations alone.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category and fix a set
$\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$ of representatives for the simple
isomorphism classes, with the tensor unit $\mathbf1$ itself representing its
class. Throughout this definition, the ordered input charges
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, total charge $d$, and all internal edge charges are labels
in $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Also fix a parenthesized binary fusion
tree. At each internal vertex with incoming charges $x,y$ and outgoing charge
$z$, choose one vector from an orthonormal basis of $V_{xy}^z$. An
**admissible labeling** assigns a representative charge to each internal edge
so that each chosen vertex basis is nonempty; a separate multiplicity-basis
index is retained at every vertex. Compose the vertex morphisms, inserting the
associators required by the chosen tree, to obtain a morphism from the
parenthesized input tensor to $d$. These composite morphisms are the
**fusion-tree vectors**. The family is called a **fusion-tree basis** when it
is an orthonormal basis of the fixed-input, fixed-total fusion space. For the
empty input list the tensor is $\mathbf1$ and its empty tree vector is
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}$ when $d=\mathbf1$; for one input $a_1$, the
only tree vector is $\operatorname{id}_{a_1}$ when $d=a_1$. The next local
lemma proves the basis property for every finite input list and includes the
dimension recursion ([[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]]).

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category, let $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$
be the representative set fixed in [[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]], and take
$a_1,\ldots,a_n,d\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Fix any parenthesized
binary tree $T$ on the ordered input list. The fusion-tree vectors of
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]] form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{Hom}(T,d)$. For $n\ge2$, their number is

$$m_T(d)=\sum_{\substack{\ell\text{ admissible, with every internal label in }\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)}}\;\prod_{v\,\mathrm{internal}}N_{\ell(v_L)\,\ell(v_R)}^{\ell(v)},$$

where the sum runs over charge labelings only (the product counts the
vertex multiplicity indices), the leaves carry the inputs, the root carries
$d$, and each internal edge is labeled by a representative simple charge.
For the empty tree, $m_0(d)=1$ if $d=\mathbf1$ and $0$ otherwise; for one
input, $m_1(d)=1$ if $a_1=d$ and $0$ otherwise. The left-associated tree on
$n\ge2$ inputs satisfies

$$m_n(d)=\sum_e m_{n-1}(e)N_{e a_n}^d\qquad(n\ge2).$$

Let $(\mathcal C,\otimes,\mathbf 1,\alpha,\lambda,\rho)$ be a monoidal
category ([[def-monoidal-category]]).

A **braiding** on $\mathcal C$ is a natural isomorphism

$$c_{X,Y}:X\otimes Y\longrightarrow Y\otimes X$$

natural in both variables ([[def-natural-isomorphism]]) such that, for all
objects $X,Y,Z$,

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}=(1_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z}\circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes1_Z),$$

and

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1}=(c_{X,Z}\otimes1_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1}\circ(1_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

These are the two **hexagon identities**. The invertibility of each
$c_{X,Y}$ is part of the data, not a consequence of the hexagons.

Every F-symbol matrix in orthonormal fusion-tree bases of a unitary fusion
category is unitary.

In a unitary braided fusion category, every R-symbol matrix in orthonormal
multiplicity bases is unitary.

Let $a,b,c,d$ be four simple input charges and $t$ a simple total charge. The
root associator identity

$$\alpha_{a,b,c\otimes d}\circ\alpha_{a\otimes b,c,d} =(\operatorname{id}_a\otimes\alpha_{b,c,d})\circ\alpha_{a,b\otimes c,d} \circ(\alpha_{a,b,c}\otimes\operatorname{id}_d)$$

has equal matrices along its two routes in the fusion-tree bases. If $A_1,A_2,A_3$
are the three successive matrices on the right and $A_4,A_5$ the two successive
matrices on the left, then

$$A_3A_2A_1=A_5A_4.$$

Each matrix coefficient sums over every intermediate simple charge and every
multiplicity-basis index.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary braided fusion category with associator $\alpha$ and
braiding $c$. For all objects $X,Y,Z$, its two hexagons are

$$\alpha_{Y,Z,X}\circ c_{X,Y\otimes Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z} =(\operatorname{id}_Y\otimes c_{X,Z})\circ\alpha_{Y,X,Z} \circ(c_{X,Y}\otimes\operatorname{id}_Z),$$

$$\alpha_{Z,X,Y}^{-1}\circ c_{X\otimes Y,Z}\circ\alpha_{X,Y,Z}^{-1} =(c_{X,Z}\otimes\operatorname{id}_Y)\circ\alpha_{X,Z,Y}^{-1} \circ(\operatorname{id}_X\otimes c_{Y,Z}).$$

For simple input charges and a fixed simple total charge, the two route matrices
in each equation are equal in fusion-tree coordinates. Each entry is the sum
over all intermediate simple charges and multiplicity indices of the products
of the corresponding F- and R-block entries.

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The next theorem proves that this maximum exists and equals the largest
singular value.

The function induced by an inner product satisfies, for all vectors $u,v$ and scalars $\lambda$,

$$\lVert v\rVert\ge0,\qquad \lVert v\rVert=0\Longleftrightarrow v=0,$$

$$\lVert\lambda v\rVert=|\lambda|\lVert v\rVert,\qquad \lVert u+v\rVert\le\lVert u\rVert+\lVert v\rVert.$$

Let $\mathbb T:=\{z\in\mathbb C:|z|=1\}$ carry the subspace topology of
$\mathbb C$ ([[def-subspace-topology-top]],
[[def-complex-metric-convergence-and-continuity]]) and the multiplication of
$\mathbb C$, and let $\varepsilon:\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\to\mathbb T$,
$\varepsilon([t]):=\exp(2\pi i t)$, for the published one-dimensional torus
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ ([[def-the-one-dimensional-torus-and-normalized-haar-integral]]).
Then $\mathbb T$ is a compact metrizable topological abelian group
([[def-topological-group]]), $\varepsilon$ is an isomorphism of topological
groups, and
$$|zw-z|=|w-1|,\qquad |z^{-1}-w^{-1}|=|z-w|$$
for all $z,w\in\mathbb T$.

Let $(X,d)$ be a nonempty compact metric space ([[def-metric-compactness]],
[[def-metric-space]]) and let $f : X \to \mathbb{R}$ be continuous
([[def-metric-continuity]]), $\mathbb{R}$ carrying its usual metric
$d_{\mathbb{R}}(s,t) = |s-t|$ ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]). Then the
image $f[X]$ is bounded above and below ([[def-bounded-set]]), and it has a
maximum and a minimum ([[def-max-min]]): there are points
$x_{\max}, x_{\min} \in X$ with

$$f(x_{\min}) \;\le\; f(x) \;\le\; f(x_{\max}) \qquad \text{for every } x \in X,$$

and then $f(x_{\max}) = \sup f[X]$ and $f(x_{\min}) = \inf f[X]$
([[def-complete-ordered-field]], [[def-infimum]]).

Nonemptiness of $X$ is a hypothesis and not an oversight: for $X = \emptyset$ the
image is empty and has neither a supremum nor a maximum. No choice principle is
used.

vector $x$, $\|(S+T)x\|\le\|Sx\|+\|Tx\|\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}+\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$,
so taking the maximum gives $\|S+T\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}+
\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Scalar homogeneity follows from [F2] and the same
maximum definition. Thus
$|\|S\|_{\mathrm{op}}-\|T\|_{\mathrm{op}}|\le\|S-T\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ by applying
the triangle inequality twice. [F1, F2, algebra]

The formula is independent of representatives. If $A'=uA$ and $B'=vB$
with $|u|=|v|=1$, then
$\inf_{|z|=1}\|A'-zB'\|=\inf_{|z|=1}\|A-(u^{-1}zv)B\|$; as $z$ runs over the
unit circle, so does $u^{-1}zv$. [given, F1, algebra]

The map $z\mapsto\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}$ is continuous: step 1.1 bounds
$|\|A-zB\|-\|A-wB\||\le\|(z-w)B\|=|z-w|\|B\|$. By [F3] and [F4] it attains
its minimum on the unit circle, so the infimum in the definition is a
minimum. Nonnegativity and symmetry follow from the norm axioms and the
substitution $z\mapsto\bar z$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]

For classes $[A],[B],[C]$, choose minimizing phases $z,w$ for the pairs
$(A,B)$ and $(B,C)$ by [F3]–[F4]. The triangle inequality gives
$\|A-zwC\|\le\|A-zB\|+\|zB-zwC\|=d_P([A],[B])+d_P([B],[C])$, so taking the
minimum over phases for $(A,C)$ proves the triangle inequality. If
$d_P([A],[B])=0$, a minimizing phase satisfies $A=zB$, so $[A]=[B]$.
Conversely equal classes have distance zero. Therefore $d_P$ is a metric on
$PU(V)$. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, step 1.2, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

projector, $U\in U(\mathcal C)$ a logical target, and $W\in U(V)$ an ambient

against the target; the second measures transfer from the code into its

Let $T:V\to W$ be a linear map between finite-dimensional real or complex inner
product spaces. If $V=0$, define $\lVert T\rVert:=0$. If $V\ne0$, define the
**operator norm** of $T$ by

$$\lVert T\rVert:=\max\{\lVert Tv\rVert:\lVert v\rVert=1\}.$$

The displayed tensor powers are tensor maps on the ordered factors, using [[def-qc-tensor-map]].
Fix an integer $n\ge 1$. Let $\mathcal H_n=Q_2^{\otimes n}$ be the ordered tensor register of $n$ qubits from [[def-qc-tensor-register-and-permutation]], and let $\mathbb F_2=\mathbb Z/2\mathbb Z$. For $x,z\in\mathbb F_2^n$, set $X^x=\bigotimes_{j=1}^n X^{x_j}$ and $Z^z=\bigotimes_{j=1}^n Z^{z_j}$, where an exponent $0$ means the identity on that factor and an exponent $1$ means the displayed Pauli matrix. $$P(k,x,z):=i^kX^xZ^z.$$

$$\mathcal C_n:=\{U\text{ unitary on }\mathcal H_n:U\mathcal P_nU^*=\mathcal P_n\}.$$

Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$U(V)$ be its unitary group. Two unitaries are **projectively equivalent**
when $A=zB$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with $|z|=1$; write $[A]\in PU(V)$ for

Let $m\ge2$ and let $\mathcal H=(\mathbb C^2)^{\otimes m}$. A **Majorana
system of length $2m$** is a family of operators
$\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_{2m}\in\operatorname{End}(\mathcal H)$ satisfying
$$\gamma_j^*=\gamma_j,\qquad \gamma_j^2=I,\qquad \gamma_j\gamma_k=-\gamma_k\gamma_j\quad(j\ne k).$$

$$Q_1(j)=\frac{I-i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}}2,\qquad Q_\psi(j)=\frac{I+i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}}2,\qquad U_j=\exp\!\left(-\frac\pi4\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}\right).$$

Since each product $\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ commutes with $\Pi$, every $U_j$, being a function of that product, preserves both parity sectors.

Put $A_j=i\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$. Then $A_j^*=A_j$ and $A_j^2=I$, so $Q_1=(I-A_j)/2$ and $Q_\psi=(I+A_j)/2$ are orthogonal complementary projections. The operator $U_j=2^{-1/2}(I-\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1})$ has eigenvalues $e^{-i\pi/4}$ on $Q_1$ and $e^{i\pi/4}$ on $Q_\psi$, whose ratio is $i$. By [F3], the channel exchange is therefore $(R_1e^{i\pi/4})U_j$; its common scalar has no effect on conjugation.

Let $c=s=2^{-1/2}$ and $A=\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$, so $U_j=cI-sA$ and $U_j^*=cI+sA$. Multiplication using $\gamma_jA=\gamma_{j+1}$, $A\gamma_j=-\gamma_{j+1}$, $\gamma_{j+1}A=-\gamma_j$, and $A\gamma_{j+1}=\gamma_j$ gives $U_j\gamma_jU_j^*=\gamma_{j+1}$ and $U_j\gamma_{j+1}U_j^*=-\gamma_j$. Every other $\gamma_k$ commutes with $A$, so $U_j\gamma_kU_j^*=\gamma_k$.

For $A=\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ and $B=\gamma_{j+1}\gamma_{j+2}$, the Majorana relations give $A^2=B^2=-I$ and $AB=-BA$. Expanding with these identities gives $$U_jU_{j+1}U_j=-(A+B)/\sqrt2=U_{j+1}U_jU_{j+1}.$$ If $|j-k|\ge2$, then the two products $\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}$ and $\gamma_k\gamma_{k+1}$ commute because moving their four distinct factors past each other contributes sign $(-1)^4=1$; hence $U_jU_k=U_kU_j$. Thus the $U_j$ satisfy the Artin braid relations. The common scalar in step 1.2 preserves these relations, since both sides of each relation have the same number of generators.

Each bilinear is a Hermitian involution; the bilinears in a fixed $\bar X_k$ have disjoint supports and commute, so every $\bar X_k$ is also a Hermitian involution. All these even monomials commute with $\Pi$ and preserve $\mathcal H_\eta$. Their supports show that the $\bar Z_j$ commute with one another, the $\bar X_k$ commute with one another, and $\bar Z_j$ anticommutes with $\bar X_k$ exactly when $j=k$ (their support intersection has odd size exactly in that case). Thus every even Majorana monomial restricts to an element of the logical phase-aware Pauli group generated by the $\bar Z_k,\bar X_k$. A finite subgroup is closed in a metric space, so this braid subgroup is not dense.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category and fix a set
$\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$ of representatives for the simple
isomorphism classes, with the tensor unit $\mathbf1$ itself representing its
class. Throughout this definition, the ordered input charges
$a_1,\ldots,a_n$, total charge $d$, and all internal edge charges are labels
in $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Also fix a parenthesized binary fusion
tree. At each internal vertex with incoming charges $x,y$ and outgoing charge
$z$, choose one vector from an orthonormal basis of $V_{xy}^z$. An
**admissible labeling** assigns a representative charge to each internal edge
so that each chosen vertex basis is nonempty; a separate multiplicity-basis
index is retained at every vertex. Compose the vertex morphisms, inserting the
associators required by the chosen tree, to obtain a morphism from the
parenthesized input tensor to $d$. These composite morphisms are the
**fusion-tree vectors**. The family is called a **fusion-tree basis** when it
is an orthonormal basis of the fixed-input, fixed-total fusion space. For the
empty input list the tensor is $\mathbf1$ and its empty tree vector is
$\operatorname{id}_{\mathbf1}$ when $d=\mathbf1$; for one input $a_1$, the
only tree vector is $\operatorname{id}_{a_1}$ when $d=a_1$. The next local
lemma proves the basis property for every finite input list and includes the
dimension recursion ([[lem-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-dimension]]).

Let $\mathcal C$ be a unitary fusion category, let $\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$
be the representative set fixed in [[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]], and take
$a_1,\ldots,a_n,d\in\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)$. Fix any parenthesized
binary tree $T$ on the ordered input list. The fusion-tree vectors of
[[def-qc-tqc-fusion-tree-basis]] form an orthonormal basis of
$\operatorname{Hom}(T,d)$. For $n\ge2$, their number is

$$m_T(d)=\sum_{\substack{\ell\text{ admissible, with every internal label in }\operatorname{Irr}(\mathcal C)}}\;\prod_{v\,\mathrm{internal}}N_{\ell(v_L)\,\ell(v_R)}^{\ell(v)},$$

where the sum runs over charge labelings only (the product counts the
vertex multiplicity indices), the leaves carry the inputs, the root carries
$d$, and each internal edge is labeled by a representative simple charge.
For the empty tree, $m_0(d)=1$ if $d=\mathbf1$ and $0$ otherwise; for one
input, $m_1(d)=1$ if $a_1=d$ and $0$ otherwise. The left-associated tree on
$n\ge2$ inputs satisfies

$$m_n(d)=\sum_e m_{n-1}(e)N_{e a_n}^d\qquad(n\ge2).$$

$\mathcal C=\mathbb C^k$ with its ordered orthonormal computational basis,
where $k\ge1$. A **fixed-charge encoding** is an isometry
$J:\mathcal C\to V$, so $J^*J=I_{\mathcal C}$. Its code subspace is
$J\mathcal C$, and its code projector is
$$P:=JJ^*:V\to V.$$
An encoding records a chosen subspace of a fusion space; it does not identify
that subspace with an object of the fusion category.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a fusion category over $\mathbb C$ in the sense of
[[def-fusion-and-multifusion-category]]. A **dagger structure** assigns to every
morphism $f:X\to Y$ a morphism $f^\dagger:Y\to X$, conjugate-linearly, with
$(g\circ f)^\dagger=f^\dagger\circ g^\dagger$ and
$(f^\dagger)^\dagger=f$. A **unitary fusion category** is such a fusion
category equipped with this dagger so that every morphism space is a
finite-dimensional normed space, composition is submultiplicative,
$\|f^\dagger\|=\|f\|$, and $\|f^\dagger f\|=\|f\|^2$. Thus each
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra.
Positive endomorphisms are the elements of its usual $C^*$-positive cone
(equivalently $u^\dagger u$ for an endomorphism $u$); in particular, if $c$ is
simple and $\operatorname{End}(c)=\mathbb C\operatorname{id}_c$, then
$\lambda\operatorname{id}_c$ is positive exactly when $\lambda\ge0$. For any
morphism $f:X\to Y$, $f^\dagger f$ is positive in $\operatorname{End}(X)$;
also require $f^\dagger f=0$ to imply $f=0$. Semisimple direct-sum

$i_j^\dagger i_j=\operatorname{id}$, and $\sum_j i_j i_j^\dagger=\operatorname{id}$.

constraints are **unitary**, meaning $\alpha^\dagger=\alpha^{-1}$,
$\lambda^\dagger=\lambda^{-1}$, and $\rho^\dagger=\rho^{-1}$.

morphisms satisfy the duality zig-zag identities. Those morphisms are not
required to be unitary isomorphisms. A braiding is additional structure; when
it is specified as a **unitary braiding**, each component satisfies
$c_{X,Y}^\dagger=c_{X,Y}^{-1}$. Positivity and unitarity are extra structure,
not consequences of the fusion rules or of the braid relations alone.

Let $H$ be a nonzero finite-dimensional complex inner-product space with the root pairing linear in the first argument. For nonzero $x\in H$, put $u=x/\|x\|$. Consequently, for every finite POVM $(E_a)_{a\in\Omega}$ on $H$, each defined outcome probability satisfies

$$\operatorname{tr}(|u\rangle\langle u|E_a)=\operatorname{tr}(|\lambda u\rangle\langle\lambda u|E_a).$$

The unnormalized vector $x$ itself gives $\operatorname{tr}(|x\rangle\langle x|)=\|x\|^2$ and is not a density operator when $\|x\|\ne1$.

Let $V\ne0$ be a finite-dimensional complex inner-product space and let
$U(V)$ be its unitary group. Two unitaries are **projectively equivalent**
when $A=zB$ for some $z\in\mathbb C$ with $|z|=1$; write $[A]\in PU(V)$ for
the equivalence class. Define
$$d_P([A],[B]):=\min_{|z|=1}\|A-zB\|_{\mathrm{op}}.$$
This is the distance after quotienting by one common scalar phase. The phase
is minimized over the unit circle; it is not chosen independently in
different charge blocks.

Let $n \in \mathbb{N}$ with $n \ge 1$, let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the set of functions
$n \to \mathbb{R}$ and let $d_2$ be the Euclidean metric on it
([[lem-metrics-on-rn]]). Then:

1. **Closed boxes are compact.** For reals $a_k \le b_k$ $(k < n)$ the box
   $Q = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_k \le x_k \le b_k \text{ for every } k < n \,\}$
   is a compact subset of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ ([[def-metric-compactness]]).
2. **Heine-Borel.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_2)$ if and only if $K$ is closed in $\mathbb{R}^n$
   ([[def-metric-topology]]) and bounded
   ([[def-metric-bounded-diameter]]).
3. **The real line.** A subset $K \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ is a compact subset of
   $(\mathbb{R}, d_{\mathbb{R}})$, the usual metric $d_{\mathbb{R}}(x,y) = |x-y|$
   ([[lem-real-line-is-a-metric-space]]), if and only if $K$ is closed in
   $\mathbb{R}$ and bounded.

**No choice principle is used.** The bisection below halves one coordinate at a
time and takes the **left** half whenever the left half still fails to be finitely
covered, the right half otherwise: a rule with two outcomes, decided by a
property of the box, not a selection. That is the whole reason the theorem is
available in ZF, while the general "complete and totally bounded implies compact"
([[thm-complete-and-totally-bounded-implies-compact]]) is not.

The hypothesis $n \ge 1$ is inherited from [[lem-metrics-on-rn]], which defines
$\mathbb{R}^n$ and its metrics only there; the last remark below records what
happens at $n = 0$.

Let $(X, \mathcal{T})$ be a Hausdorff topological space
([[def-hausdorff-space]], [[def-topological-space]]), with compact subsets as in
[[def-compact-space]]. Then:

1. **A point and a disjoint compact set are separated.** If $K \subseteq X$ is
   compact and $x \in X \setminus K$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$x \in U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
2. **Two disjoint compact sets are separated.** If $K, L \subseteq X$ are compact
   and $K \cap L = \varnothing$, there are $U, V \in \mathcal{T}$ with
   $$L \subseteq U, \qquad K \subseteq V, \qquad U \cap V = \varnothing .$$
3. **Compact implies closed.** Every compact subset of $X$ is closed in $X$.
4. **In a compact Hausdorff space the two classes coincide.** If in addition
   $(X, \mathcal{T})$ is compact, then a subset of $X$ is compact if and only if
   it is closed.

**The proof is written choice-free, and that is not a stylistic preference.** The
textbook argument says "for each $y \in K$ choose disjoint open $U_y, V_y$",
which is a selection over an arbitrary index set and therefore an appeal to the
full Axiom of Choice. What is done below instead is to take the family of **all**
open $V$ that admit some open $U \ni x$ disjoint from them — a family cut out by
a formula, with nothing selected — extract a finite subcover from it, and only
then make finitely many selections, which [[lem-finite-choice]] supplies as a
theorem of ZF.

The map $t\mapsto(\cos t,\sin t)$ is a bijection from $[0,2\pi)$ onto $S^1=\{(x,y)\in\mathbb R^2:x^2+y^2=1\}$. conjugation on the imaginary quaternions defines a surjective two-sheeted
covering homomorphism

$$\rho:SU(2)\longrightarrow SO(3),\qquad \rho(q)(v)=qvq^{-1},$$

whose kernel is $\{1,-1\}$.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by

The determinant of a unitary $A\in U(2)$ has modulus one, since
$1=\det(A^*A)=\overline{\det A}\det A$. Write $\det A=e^{i\theta}$ by [F4]
and put $\lambda=e^{-i\theta/2}$. Then $|\lambda|=1$ and
$\det(\lambda A)=\lambda^2\det A=1$, so $\lambda A\in SU(2)$ and
$q(\lambda A)=q(A)$. Thus $q$ is onto. [given, F4, algebra]

If $A\in SU(2)$ and $q(A)=[I]$, then $A=\lambda I$ for some $|\lambda|=1$.
The determinant condition gives $\lambda^2=1$, hence $\lambda=\pm1$.
Conversely $I$ and $-I$ have the same projective class. Therefore
$\ker q=\{\pm I\}$, and two matrices have the same $q$-image exactly when
they differ by this kernel. [given, step 1.1, algebra]

The map $q$ is continuous: by [F1],
$d_P(q(A),q(B))\le\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}$. Identify $M_2(\mathbb C)$ with
$\mathbb R^8$. The equations $A^*A=I$ and $\det A=1$ define a closed subset,
and each matrix entry is bounded in modulus by $1$ because each column has
norm $1$. Thus $SU(2)$ is compact by [F2]. The metric space $PU(2)$ is
Hausdorff by [F1]. If $F\subseteq SU(2)$ is closed, then it is compact and
$q(F)$ is compact, hence closed by [F3]. It is a quotient map: if $q^{-1}(W)$ is open, then
$q^{-1}(PU(2)\setminus W)$ is closed; surjectivity and closedness of $q$
make its image $PU(2)\setminus W$ closed, so $W$ is open. [F1, F2, F3, step 1.1, algebra]

By [F5] and step 2.1, $q$ and $\rho$ have exactly the same fibers.
There is therefore a unique bijective group homomorphism
$\bar\rho:PU(2)\to SO(3)$ with $\bar\rho(q(A))=\rho(A)$. It is continuous
because $q$ is a quotient map and $\rho=\bar\rho\circ q$ is continuous.
The space $PU(2)=q(SU(2))$ is compact, while $SO(3)$ is Hausdorff as a
subspace of the real $3\times3$ matrix space. A continuous bijection from
a compact space to a Hausdorff space is a homeomorphism: images of closed
sets are compact and therefore closed by [F3]. Hence $\bar\rho$ is a
topological group isomorphism. Since $q$ is a quotient map and its fibers
are exactly the cosets of $\{\pm I\}$ by step 2.1, the induced map
$SU(2)/\{\pm I\}\to PU(2)$ is also a homeomorphism. The covering sheets
for $q$ are carried from those of $\rho$ by this homeomorphism, so $q$ is a
two-sheeted covering.
[A1, F3, F5, step 2.1, step 2.2, algebra] ∎

$$U_j=\exp(-\pi\gamma_j\gamma_{j+1}/4),\qquad 1\le j<2m.$$

qubits. Their braid-only projective image is finite and is not dense in

Its parity operator is $\Pi=i^m\gamma_1\cdots\gamma_{2m}$. For each adjacent

$\|f^\dagger\|=\|f\|$, and $\|f^\dagger f\|=\|f\|^2$. Thus each
$\operatorname{End}_{\mathcal C}(X)$ is a finite-dimensional $C^*$-algebra.
Positive endomorphisms are the elements of its usual $C^*$-positive cone
(equivalently $u^\dagger u$ for an endomorphism $u$); in particular, if $c$ is
simple and $\operatorname{End}(c)=\mathbb C\operatorname{id}_c$, then
$\lambda\operatorname{id}_c$ is positive exactly when $\lambda\ge0$. For any
morphism $f:X\to Y$, $f^\dagger f$ is positive in $\operatorname{End}(X)$;
also require $f^\dagger f=0$ to imply $f=0$. Semisimple direct-sum
decompositions can be chosen orthogonally:
their inclusions $i_j$ satisfy $i_j^\dagger i_k=0$ for $j\ne k$,
$i_j^\dagger i_j=\operatorname{id}$, and $\sum_j i_j i_j^\dagger=\operatorname{id}$.
Tensor product preserves daggers:
$(f\otimes g)^\dagger=f^\dagger\otimes g^\dagger$. Its associator and unit
constraints are **unitary**, meaning $\alpha^\dagger=\alpha^{-1}$,
$\lambda^\dagger=\lambda^{-1}$, and $\rho^\dagger=\rho^{-1}$.

The underlying fusion category is rigid, so its evaluation and coevaluation

required to be unitary isomorphisms. A braiding is additional structure; when
it is specified as a **unitary braiding**, each component satisfies
$c_{X,Y}^\dagger=c_{X,Y}^{-1}$. Positivity and unitarity are extra structure,
not consequences of the fusion rules or of the braid relations alone.

$V=\operatorname{Hom}(a^{\otimes n},d)$, satisfy the Artin relations, and
define a unitary representation $\rho:B_n\to U(V)$, where $U(V)$ is the group
of invertible linear maps preserving the inner product on $V$.

computation; under coherent control it is a relative phase and must be
tracked.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.
